tabs.title: Argumentative Nuance
tabs.description: Analyse the author's distinctions and concessions.

tabs.title: Conceptual Critique
tabs.description: Examine the limits of institutional indicators.

tabs.title: Evaluative Transfer
tabs.description: Judge complex cases using evidence from the text.

questions.q: What is the effect of describing resilience as an ideal 'difficult to oppose'?
choices: It dismisses resilience as fashionable but intellectually empty.
It suggests that most teachers disagree about the term's meaning.
It establishes the ideal's appeal before questioning its institutional misuse.
It implies that criticism of resilience is necessarily contradictory.
questions.explanation: The opening grants resilience's appeal before distinguishing a useful capacity from an imposed moral expectation.

questions.q: What conceptual distinction does the example of the two pupils primarily sharpen?
choices: The contrast between agency exercised with prospects of change and endurance demanded despite inadequate support.
The difference between academic achievement and emotional intelligence.
The contrast between visible effort and the reliability of standardised assessments.
The difference between practical assistance and moral encouragement.
questions.explanation: Both pupils can appear determined, but only one has realistic conditions under which effort can produce change.

questions.q: Why does the author reject a return to the idea of fixed talent?
choices: It would remove every incentive to introduce better assessment metrics.
It would require abandoning all institutional responsibility.
It would make perseverance an even stronger moral imperative.
It would mistake criticism of compulsory resilience for a denial of learner agency.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph explicitly preserves the value of agency while rejecting a simplistic resilience ideal.

questions.q: Why is the assessment indicator described as 'not necessarily false'?
choices: Its numerical precision is presumed to establish its educational value.
It may accurately capture rate of score improvement while missing other forms of learning.
It can only be evaluated after all learners reach the same benchmark.
Its validity depends solely on whether learners know the scoring rules.
questions.explanation: The indicator answers the narrow question of score improvement, not the full value of difficult inquiry.

questions.q: What is implied by the claim that performance indicators can 'colonise' activities?
choices: Measures can begin to redefine what participants consider worthwhile.
School subjects are likely to become increasingly specialised.
Students will inevitably reject all activities without a score.
Institutional metrics make informal learning easier to compare.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three argues that a metric can take over the meaning of activities it was designed to illuminate.

questions.q: What institutional risk accompanies praise for a pupil's visible endurance?
choices: It prevents teachers from noticing genuine academic progress.
It makes every pupil less willing to ask for help.
It may distract from asking why the adverse conditions persist.
It establishes that continued effort always leads to success.
questions.explanation: The writer warns that celebrating endurance can spare institutions the obligation to examine ongoing obstacles.

questions.q: A student abandons an unproductive project after carefully reconsidering its aims. What would the author most likely infer?
choices: The decision demonstrates a lack of resilience regardless of context.
The student has confused motivation with a measurable goal.
The project should be resumed until its failure can be quantified.
The choice can reflect mature judgement rather than a deficit in perseverance.
questions.explanation: The author argues that knowing when persistence ceases to serve a purpose is part of mature learning.

questions.q: A college introduces flexible deadlines but still requires students to justify every period of rest. Which criticism best follows from the text?
choices: Flexible deadlines eliminate the need to evaluate students.
The institution still treats rest as a failure of ambition rather than a legitimate need.
Students will necessarily use the flexibility to reduce effort.
Any assessment of progress becomes incompatible with student choice.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph explicitly calls for treating rest as more than a failure of ambition.

questions.q: Two equally determined learners make unequal progress because one lacks support. What would be an unwarranted inference?
choices: The slower learner necessarily lacks the character required for academic success.
The conditions under which effort is applied should be examined.
Both students might still benefit from revising their strategies.
Visible determination does not reveal the entire educational situation.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph rejects interpreting unequal resources as a difference in moral character.

questions.q: Which principle most accurately integrates the author's recommendations?
choices: Reward endurance whenever it can be documented, but permit exceptions.
Eliminate performance measures so learners can develop freely.
Provide conditions that make effort meaningful while retaining freedom to reconsider one's goals.
Replace academic evaluation with individual assessments of motivation.
questions.explanation: The conclusion advocates enabling conditions and the freedom to reconsider worthwhile aims while preserving discerning evaluation.
